validated_results.title: Relationship between plasma carotenoids and prostate cancer.
validated_results.reason: Case-control analysis of plasma trans-beta-carotene and prostate cancer risk in men, reporting an inverse association with incident (nonmetastatic) prostate cancer.

extraction.population: men with nonmetastatic prostate cancer and healthy men from the same area

sample_size.excerpt: Comparing 118 non-Hispanic Caucasian men mainly from southeast Texas with nonmetastatic prostate cancer with 52 healthy men from the same area, we conducted a case-control analysis evaluating associations between risk and plasma levels of total carotenoids, beta-cryptoxanthin, alpha- and trans-beta-carotene, lutein and zeaxanthin, total lycopenes, trans-lycopene, total cis-lycopenes, and cis-lycopene isoforms 1, 2, 3, and 5.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 118 + 52 = 170

cases.excerpt: Comparing 118 non-Hispanic Caucasian men mainly from southeast Texas with nonmetastatic prostate cancer with 52 healthy men from the same area, we conducted a case-control analysis evaluating associations between risk and plasma levels of total carotenoids, beta-cryptoxanthin, alpha- and trans-beta-carotene, lutein and zeaxanthin, total lycopenes, trans-lycopene, total cis-lycopenes, and cis-lycopene isoforms 1, 2, 3, and 5.

effect_size.excerpt: Risk for men with high plasma levels of alpha-carotene, trans-beta-carotene, beta-cryptoxanthin, and lutein and zeaxanthin was less than half that for those with lower levels.

design.excerpt: we conducted a case-control analysis evaluating associations between risk and plasma levels of total carotenoids

timing.excerpt: we conducted a case-control analysis evaluating associations between risk and plasma levels

exposure_measurement.excerpt: plasma levels of total carotenoids, beta-cryptoxanthin, alpha- and trans-beta-carotene

parallel_r3_gate_reasons: JBI remains Fair after Claude R2
important quantitative evidence remains missing or invalid: ci_lower, ci_upper, effect_size, effect_type, p_value

validated_results.title: Milk, dairy products and cancer risk (Italy).
validated_results.reason: Hospital-based case-control study in Italy reporting a prostate cancer odds ratio for the highest consumption level of milk and dairy products.

extraction.comparison_type: highest vs lowest consumption level of any type of milk
extraction.population: hospital-based cases of prostate cancer and controls

sample_size.excerpt: We analyzed data from a large and integrated network of hospital-based case-control studies in Italy on cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx (598 cases, 1491 controls), oesophagus (304 cases, 743 controls), colorectum (1953 cases, 4154 controls), larynx (460 cases, 1088 controls), breast (2569 cases, 2588 controls), ovary (1031 cases, 2411 controls) and prostate (1294 cases, 1451 controls).
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 1294 + 1451 = 2745

cases.excerpt: We analyzed data from a large and integrated network of hospital-based case-control studies in Italy on cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx (598 cases, 1491 controls), oesophagus (304 cases, 743 controls), colorectum (1953 cases, 4154 controls), larynx (460 cases, 1088 controls), breast (2569 cases, 2588 controls), ovary (1031 cases, 2411 controls) and prostate (1294 cases, 1451 controls).

effect_size.excerpt: Multivariate odds ratio (OR) for the highest consumption level of any type of milk was 0.94 (95% confidence interval, CI: 0.61-1.33) for cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx, 1.20 (95% CI: 0.76-1.90) for oesophageal, 0.77 (95% CI: 0.62-0.96) for colon, 0.80 (95% CI: 0.60-1.05) for rectal, 0.83 (95% CI: 0.56-1.21) for laryngeal, 0.91 (95% CI: 0.76-1.10) for breast, 0.89 (95% CI: 0.68-1.15) for ovarian and 1.08 (95% CI: 0.84-1.37) for prostate cancer. A significant trend in risk was found for colon cancer only.
